meta.blurb: Elif eats takeaway, ready meals and desk snacks, and every headline tells her something different. Her uncle Davit, a cook for forty years, gives her simple rules for shopping, cooking and eating well, with no diet and no guilt.
meta.bible: Elif: a busy, curious engineer of thirty-four who eats mostly takeaway and ready meals and is confused by food headlines. Davit: her uncle, a cook for forty years, warm, practical and allergic to fads. Nina: Elif's colleague who becomes her lunch partner. They cook in Davit's small Kitchen over one month, and shop at the Saturday Market and a supermarket. Key terms: Ultra-processed food, Fibre, Whole grains, Pulses, Ingredients list, Nutrition table, Dietitian, Mediterranean. Facts used: the World Health Organization advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day (about five portions), less than five grams of salt a day, and free sugars below ten percent of energy, with below five percent better. Adults are often advised to eat about 25 to 30 grams of fibre a day. Processed meat is linked with a higher risk of bowel cancer. A small, careful trial in the United States in 2019 found that people ate about 500 more calories a day on an ultra-processed diet than on an unprocessed one, and gained a little weight in two weeks. Voice: kind, practical and never preachy; no foods are labelled good or bad; the science is real and hedged where it is uncertain; no invented numbers or studies. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: At nine o'clock Elif opens her empty fridge for the third time that week. She sighs, picks up her phone and orders takeaway again, while a headline on the screen tells her that eggs are bad for her.
Elif's uncle Davit has been a cook for forty years. When she tells him about her confusion, he laughs and says that eating well is much simpler than the headlines make it seem.
Davit explains why the headlines keep changing, and the reason is simple. Food is hard to study, because people eat thousands of different things and they rarely remember exactly what they ate.

Davit says that the overall pattern matters more than any single food. Most experts agree that diets with plenty of vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains, and little heavily processed food, are good for health.
Davit announces rule one, which is to cook most of your own meals. Elif starts with an omelette and a salad, and it takes her fifteen minutes.
When you cook at home, you decide how much salt, sugar and fat goes into the pot. Some studies link home cooking with a healthier diet, although people who cook may also differ in other ways.
Cooking does not have to be fancy, says Davit, and five easy meals are enough to start. If Elif can make eggs, a bean stew, pasta, a stir-fry and soup, she can feed herself all week.
Davit shows her how to cook extra and freeze it in small boxes. On a busy evening she can warm a home-made meal in five minutes, which is quicker than waiting for a delivery.

In the supermarket, Davit points to packets covered with words such as natural, light and high in protein. He says that these claims on the front are the loudest part of the package, and not always the most honest.
Rule two is to turn the packet over, and Elif soon sees why. The ingredients list and the nutrition table are facts, and they are harder to dress up than the words on the front.

Ingredients are listed in order, from the largest amount to the smallest. If sugar appears near the top of the list, Davit explains, then the product is mostly sugar, however healthy the front may sound.
Elif compares two pots of yoghurt, one plain and one labelled low fat. The low-fat pot has more sugar, so Davit teaches her to compare the numbers per one hundred grams.

Davit explains that processing is not always bad, and that many processed foods are perfectly fine. Frozen peas, tinned beans, bread and plain yoghurt are all processed in some way, and they can all be part of a good diet.

Rule three is to go easy on ultra-processed foods, which come from industrial recipes with additives you would not find at home. Think of sugary drinks, many packaged snacks, instant noodles and some ready meals.

Many large studies link a diet high in ultra-processed food with poorer health. These studies cannot prove cause and effect, however, because people who eat a lot of such foods may differ in other ways.

In a small, careful trial in the United States in 2019, people were fed two different diets for two weeks each. On the ultra-processed diet they ate about 500 more calories a day, and they gained a little weight.
Davit tells her not to try to be perfect. She should swap one thing at a time, and Elif starts by replacing her afternoon crisps with an apple and a handful of nuts.
At the Saturday market, Davit announces rule four, which is to eat plenty of plants. He asks Elif to put vegetables on her plate at every meal, and not only at dinner.
The World Health Organization advises at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables a day, which is about five portions. Davit says that many adults eat less than this, and that Elif was one of them.

Davit explains that fibre, found in plants, feeds the helpful bacteria in our gut and keeps digestion moving. Adults are often advised to eat about 25 to 30 grams a day, but many people eat much less.
Davit loves pulses, which are beans, lentils and chickpeas. They are cheap, they keep for a long time, and they give fibre and protein, so Elif learns to make a lentil soup.

Davit suggests that Elif eats as many different plants as she can in a week, in as many colours as she can find. Different plants contain different nutrients, so variety is a simple way to cover many needs.

Rule five is to choose whole grains, which keep the outer layers of the grain that hold much of the fibre. Davit suggests swapping some white bread, rice and pasta for wholemeal ones, such as oats, brown rice and wholemeal bread.
Davit says that white bread is not poison and that nobody has to give it up. The goal, he says, is balance across the week, not a long list of forbidden foods.
Elif admits that she drinks two or three sugary drinks a day to keep herself going at work. Davit smiles gently and says that rule six is about what is in the glass.

Sugary drinks add many calories without making us feel full the way food does. The World Health Organization advises keeping free sugars below ten percent of our daily energy, and below five percent is even better.
Water, tea and coffee without sugar are all good choices. Fruit juice is not forbidden, but it still counts as free sugar, so Davit suggests small glasses and eating the whole fruit instead.
Rule seven is to watch the salt, and most of it comes from packaged food and not from the shaker. The World Health Organization advises less than five grams a day, about one teaspoon.

Davit says that fat is not the enemy, because not all fats are the same. Olive oil, nuts and oily fish such as sardines are widely thought to be good choices, while some processed foods contain less healthy fats.
Many health bodies recommend eating fish about twice a week, including one portion of oily fish. Davit grills sardines with lemon, and Elif is surprised by how much she likes them.
Davit reminds her that processed meats, such as bacon, sausages and ham, are linked with a higher risk of bowel cancer. He suggests keeping them modest, and making meat a smaller part of the plate.
At work, Elif eats her lunch at her desk in about five minutes, with her eyes on the screen. By the time she looks down, the sandwich is gone and she cannot say what it tasted like.
The body takes some time to send the message that it is full. If we eat very fast, we can eat more than we need before the message arrives, so slowing down can help.
Elif invites her colleague Nina to eat lunch on a bench in the park, away from the screens. They talk, they taste their food, and the hour feels like a real break.
Davit says to stop eating when you feel comfortably full. A Japanese saying suggests stopping when you are about eighty percent full, which is not a scientific rule but a useful reminder.
At Davit's birthday party, Elif eats a large slice of cake without guilt. Davit says that rule nine is that treats are part of life, and that no food is simply good or bad.
Davit suggests having treats now and then and enjoying them fully. He says that very strict rules often backfire, because people who forbid themselves a food often end up wanting it even more.
One night Elif eats a whole pizza and feels guilty. Davit tells her that one meal does not decide anyone's health, and that the important thing is to carry on at the next meal.
Rule ten is to plan ahead, so Elif writes a shopping list before she goes to the shop. She never goes when she is hungry, because hungry shoppers fill the basket with snacks.
Davit says that frozen and tinned vegetables are good choices. Frozen ones are usually frozen soon after picking, so they keep most of their nutrients, and they never go bad in the fridge.

Eating well does not have to be expensive, and many of the best foods are cheap. Beans, rice, oats, eggs and seasonal vegetables cost little, and cooking at home often costs less than buying ready meals.
On Sunday afternoons, Elif now cooks one big pot of soup or stew. It gives her lunches and dinners for most of the week, and it costs her only an hour.
Rule eleven is that no single diet is best, says Davit. Traditional diets from the Mediterranean, Japan, Mexico and India are healthy in different ways, and most are home-cooked and rich in plants.
Elif loves her grandmother's recipes, and Davit says she does not have to give them up. She can adapt them, for example with more vegetables and less salt, because food is also part of who we are.
Davit tells her to be wary of fads, superfoods and detox cures. If a product promises to fix everything and the person telling you is selling it, the claim deserves a great deal of doubt.
Rule twelve is to make peace with food, and eating should not be a source of fear. Anyone whose worries about food or weight take over their life should talk to a doctor.

Davit makes one more point, which is that these rules are general. People with allergies, diabetes or kidney disease, pregnant women and children may all need individual advice from a doctor or a dietitian.
After one month, Elif cooks most of her meals and has more energy than she used to. She has not given up any food, but she has learned a handful of simple habits that she is happy to keep.
Davit writes the rules on one page, and Elif pins it to her fridge beside her five meals. They say to cook, read the back, eat plants, drink water, slow down, enjoy treats and make peace with food.
Elif's story is meant to inform and not to treat. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please speak to a doctor or dietitian about your own needs.
C1C2: At nine o'clock on a Tuesday night, Elif opened her nearly empty fridge for the third time that week and, with a sigh, ordered takeaway again. While she waited, the news on her phone announced that a certain food was now harmful, only a month after another headline had called the same food a miracle. She did not know whom to believe, and she was far too tired to find out.

On Sunday Elif visited her uncle Davit, who had been a cook for forty years and who greeted her with a wooden spoon in one hand and a pot of soup in the other. When she described her confusion, he laughed warmly and said that the basics of eating well are much simpler than the headlines would have her believe. He offered her a month in his kitchen and a set of simple rules, with no diet, no counting and no guilt.

Food science is genuinely difficult, Davit explained, and that is why headlines swing so wildly from one week to the next. People eat thousands of different things over the years, they rarely remember exactly what was on their plates, and the people who eat one particular food often differ from other people in many other ways. A single study, he warned, is rarely the last word on any question, and the same is true of a single headline.

What matters most, Davit said, is the overall pattern of eating across the years, and not any single food or any single meal. Although experts argue about the details, most of them agree that diets rich in vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains, and low in heavily processed food, are good for long-term health. There is no secret ingredient, he added, only a way of eating that is easy to keep up.

Rule one, Davit announced, was to cook most of your own meals, and he handed Elif a pan, three eggs and a handful of herbs. Fifteen minutes later she was eating a soft, golden omelette with a salad, and she had to admit that it tasted better than anything she had ordered all month. It was not a gourmet dish, but it was hers, and she felt a small glow of pride as she washed the pan.

When you cook at home, Davit said, you decide how much salt, sugar and fat goes into the pot, and you know exactly what is in your food. Some studies link regular home cooking with a better quality of diet, although people who enjoy cooking may differ from other people in many ways. Even so, he said, it is hard to improve your eating if you never see what you are eating.

Cooking does not have to be fancy, Davit insisted, and a person who can make five simple meals can feed themselves well for a lifetime. He proposed eggs, a bean stew, pasta with vegetables, a stir-fry and a vegetable soup, all of which could be made in about half an hour with cheap ingredients. Elif wrote the list on a sticky note and put it on her fridge.

The trick for busy people, Davit said, is to cook a double portion and freeze half in small containers, so that a home-made meal is always waiting in the freezer. On a tired evening, Elif could warm one in five minutes, which was faster than any delivery and a good deal cheaper. She felt as though she had discovered a secret that everyone else had always known.

Rule two began in a supermarket aisle, where Davit stopped in front of a wall of packets covered in bold promises such as natural, light, wholesome and high in protein. The front of a packet, he said, is an advertisement, and its job is to sell, so the words on it are chosen for their effect rather than for their completeness. Elif looked at the shelves as if she were seeing them for the first time.

Rule two, Davit announced, was to turn the packet over, because the ingredients list and the nutrition table on the back are regulated facts, while the claims on the front are free to flatter. Elif picked up a cereal box that had been marketed as a healthy start to the day and, squinting at the tiny print, found that sugar was the second ingredient. She put it back on the shelf with a small, surprised laugh, and then began to turn over every packet in reach.

Ingredients, Davit explained, must be listed in order of weight, from the greatest amount to the smallest, so the first few words tell you most of what you need to know. If sugar sits near the top of the list, the product contains a lot of it, however healthy the picture on the front may look, and the same is true of salt and of various oils. It is a short skill that can be learned in an afternoon, and it can be used for the rest of one's life.

Davit handed Elif two pots of yoghurt, one with a cheerful low-fat label and one that was plain, and asked her to compare them using the nutrition table. The low-fat pot, she discovered, contained considerably more sugar, because flavour removed with the fat had been replaced with sweetness, a practice that is common but not universal. Comparing the numbers per one hundred grams, Davit said, is the fairest way to judge two products.

Not all processing is bad, Davit said, for freezing, canning, drying and baking are ancient methods that make food safer, cheaper and easier to keep. Frozen peas, tinned beans, wholemeal bread and plain yoghurt are all processed to some degree, and they all earn a place in a healthy kitchen. The word to watch for, he said, was a different one, and he led her to the next shelf.

Rule three, Davit explained, was to go easy on ultra-processed foods, which are industrial formulations made largely from refined ingredients and additives such as flavourings, colours, emulsifiers and sweeteners, which you would never find in a home kitchen. Sugary drinks, many packaged snacks, instant noodles and reconstituted meat products often fall into this group. They are designed to be cheap, long-lasting and highly appealing, he said, and they succeed at all three.

Many large studies, Davit said, have linked diets high in ultra-processed food with a greater risk of obesity, heart disease and other health problems. Such studies can only show an association and not a cause, because people who eat a great deal of these foods may also be poorer, busier or less active than others. Scientists try to adjust for those differences, but they can never be completely certain, although the same pattern appears in many countries.

In 2019, Davit said, a small but careful trial in the United States housed volunteers in a research centre and gave each of them two different diets for two weeks. When they ate the ultra-processed diet, they consumed about five hundred more calories a day than when they ate the unprocessed one, and they gained a little weight. The meals had been matched for sugar, fat and fibre on offer, yet nobody can say that one small trial settles the question, he cautioned.

Perfection, Davit warned, is the enemy of progress, and nobody needs to banish every packet from the house. He suggested that Elif change one thing at a time, and she began by replacing the afternoon crisps on her desk with an apple and a handful of nuts. Within two weeks she had stopped noticing the swap, and she was ready for the next one.

At the Saturday market, among stalls piled with leaves, roots and fruit, Davit announced rule four, which was to put plants at the centre of her plate. He asked her to include vegetables in every meal, including breakfast, and to think of meat or fish as a supporting actor rather than the star of the show. Elif bought a bag of spinach, a bunch of carrots and a ridiculous number of tomatoes.

The World Health Organization advises eating at least four hundred grams of fruit and vegetables a day, Davit said, which works out at roughly five portions. Surveys in many countries show that a large share of adults fall short of this amount, and Elif, who counted a bag of crisps as a vegetable on a bad day, knew that she was among them. A portion, he added, is roughly what fits into the palm of a hand.

Fibre, Davit said, is the part of plant food that we cannot digest, and it plays a quiet but important role, feeding the trillions of bacteria in our gut and keeping digestion moving smoothly. Adults are often advised to aim for about twenty-five to thirty grams a day, yet many people eat considerably less. High-fibre diets have been linked with a lower risk of several illnesses, though the details are still being studied.

Davit's favourite food, he confessed, was the humble pulse, which is the family that includes beans, lentils, peas and chickpeas. They are cheap, last for months in a cupboard and provide both fibre and protein, and they appear in the traditional cooking of almost every culture. Elif's first lentil soup was a little bland, but by the third attempt she was adding lemon and cumin, and her kitchen smelled wonderful.

Variety, Davit suggested, is a simple insurance policy, because different plants contain different nutrients and different kinds of fibre. He challenged Elif to eat as many different plants as she could in a week, counting vegetables, fruit, herbs, nuts, seeds and beans, and she was amazed to find how quickly the list grew. There is no magic number, he said, but the more varied the plate, the better the odds.

Rule five, Davit said, was to choose whole grains, which retain the outer layers of the seed, and those layers contain much of the fibre and many of the vitamins that refining strips away. He suggested that Elif swap some of her white bread, rice and pasta for wholemeal versions, and add oats, barley or brown rice to her week. People who eat more whole grains tend to have lower rates of heart disease, although, as always, other habits play a part.

Davit cut a thick slice of crusty white bread, spread it with butter and handed it to Elif with a grin, saying that it was not poison and that nobody should live in fear of a loaf. The aim, he said, is balance across the week and not purity at every meal, and a rule that makes you miserable is a rule that will not last. She ate the bread slowly, with the butter melting into it, and enjoyed every crumb as if it were a small holiday.

Elif admitted, a little sheepishly, that she got through her working day on two or three fizzy drinks and a sweet coffee, because they kept her going when her energy dipped. Davit did not scold her, but explained that rule six was about what is in the glass. Drinks, he said, are the easiest place to make a change, because they are the easiest place to hide sugar.

Sugary drinks, Davit said, deliver a large amount of sugar in liquid form, and the body does not seem to register those calories in the same way as those from solid food, so we do not feel fuller afterwards. The World Health Organization advises keeping free sugars below ten percent of daily energy, with below five percent giving extra benefit, and a single can of fizzy drink can use up much of that allowance. Elif looked at her half-empty bottle as though it had told her a lie, and she did not buy another that week.

Water, plain tea and coffee were the best choices, Davit said, and Elif discovered that a jug of water with lemon slices and a few mint leaves was surprisingly pleasant. Fruit juice, though it comes from fruit, counts as free sugar because the fibre has been removed, so he recommended small glasses and, when possible, eating the whole fruit instead. After a month, she noticed that she no longer craved the fizzy drinks, and her afternoons felt steadier as well.

Rule seven was to watch the salt, and Davit reminded her that in many countries most of the salt in our diets comes from bread, sauces and prepared foods and not from the shaker on the table. The World Health Organization advises that adults eat less than five grams of salt a day, which is about a level teaspoon, because a high intake is linked with raised blood pressure. Cooking at home, he said, makes it easy to taste first and add salt later.

Fat is not the enemy, Davit said, and the old habit of treating every fat as villainous has caused a great deal of confusion. Fats from olive oil, nuts, seeds and oily fish such as sardines and mackerel are widely considered to be good choices, while large amounts of the saturated fat found in many pastries and processed meats are best kept modest. The research is complicated, he admitted, but the broad pattern is quite consistent across many studies and many countries.

Many health organisations recommend eating fish about twice a week, including one portion of an oily kind, and Davit decided that it was time for a demonstration. He grilled sardines with lemon, olive oil and a pinch of salt on a small stove and served them on toast, and Elif, who had expected to dislike them, took a second helping. Tinned fish, he added, counts just as well, and it is much cheaper than fresh, so it is a fine choice for busy weeks.

Processed meats such as bacon, sausages and ham, Davit said, are linked with a higher risk of bowel cancer, and health bodies advise keeping them modest. Red meat, too, is often best eaten in moderation, though it can be a valuable source of iron and protein, and the evidence about it is less clear-cut. Elif decided to turn her usual plate around, giving the vegetables the largest share and the meat a supporting role.

At work, Elif ate her lunch in about five minutes with her eyes fixed on a screen, and by the time she looked down, the sandwich had vanished and she could not have told you what was in it. Davit, hearing about this, put down his spoon and announced rule eight, which was to slow down and sit down. Eating, he said, should be something you notice and not something that merely happens to you.

The signals that tell the brain we are full take a while to arrive, Davit explained, so a person who eats very quickly can finish a large portion before the message has even been delivered. Studies suggest that slower eating may help people to eat a little less, though the effect is modest and varies between individuals. The real gain, he said, is that you start to taste your food and to enjoy it.

Elif invited her colleague Nina to take their lunches to a bench in the park, away from every screen, and the two women ate slowly in the sunshine while they talked. The food tasted better, the break felt like a real break, and when they returned to the office, Elif was more refreshed than she had been in months. Sharing meals, Davit pointed out, is one of the oldest human habits and one of the kindest.

Stop when you are comfortably full, Davit advised, and not when the plate is empty or the stomach is stretched. A well-known Japanese saying suggests eating until you are about eighty percent full, and although it is a piece of folk wisdom and not a scientific rule, it is a helpful reminder to listen to your body. Elif found that, once she slowed down, her stomach was a surprisingly reliable guide.

At Davit's birthday party, a chocolate cake appeared with a flourish and Elif, who had been so careful all month, hesitated until her uncle pressed a large slice into her hand. Rule nine, he said with a twinkle, was that treats are part of a happy life, and that no single food should be labelled simply good or bad. Cake eaten with friends and savoured is a very different thing from cake eaten alone in a panic.

The best treats, Davit said, are those that are occasional, delicious and properly enjoyed, and he advised Elif to choose what she really loved rather than eating whatever was lying about. Very strict rules often seem to backfire, because the more firmly a food is forbidden, the more attractive it can become, though people differ a good deal in how they respond. A little of what you love, eaten with attention, rarely does harm, and it is often more satisfying than a large amount of something mediocre.

One difficult evening Elif ate an entire pizza after a terrible day, and she called Davit in a mood of deep gloom, convinced that she had ruined the whole month. He laughed kindly and told her that one meal, like one walk, does not decide a person's health, and that the only real mistake is to give up. The way to recover was beautifully simple: eat well at the next meal and move on.

Rule ten, Davit said, was to plan, and the first step was to write a shopping list on the back of an envelope before leaving the house. He also told her never to shop when she was hungry, since a hungry shopper's basket fills with snacks, whereas a planned shopper's basket fills with meals. Elif tried it on Friday and spent less money, and she finished the week with no wasted food at all.

Frozen and tinned vegetables, Davit said, deserve far more respect than they usually receive, because frozen ones are generally prepared soon after picking and keep most of their nutrients. They are also cheap, they last for months and they never rot in the bottom of the fridge, which makes them ideal for busy people. When he opened her freezer and found it full of peas, spinach and berries, he nodded with real approval.

Elif had always assumed that eating well was a luxury, but Davit showed her that the cheapest foods in the shop are often among the best. Beans, lentils, rice, oats, eggs, cabbage and seasonal vegetables cost very little, and cooking from scratch generally costs far less per portion than buying ready meals or takeaway, though it does take time. Good food, he said, is not about spending more, but about spending wisely and cooking with a little care.

A pattern had settled into Elif's week, and it began on Sunday afternoons, when she cooked one enormous pot of soup or stew while listening to music. It gave her lunches and dinners for most of the following week, it cost her only an hour of her time and it smelled so good that her neighbours began to knock on her door. Davit called this the best investment of her whole week, and he asked her for the recipe for the lentils.

Rule eleven, Davit said, was to remember that there is no single best diet, since traditional ways of eating from the Mediterranean to Japan and from Mexico to India have all supported healthy populations. They share a few features, including freshly cooked food, plenty of plants and little packaged food, but they differ wildly in flavour and ingredients. The best diet, he concluded, is a good one that you can enjoy for the rest of your life.

Elif had worried that eating well would mean abandoning her grandmother's recipes, but Davit shook his head and said that food is not only fuel but also memory, identity and love. She did not need to give up the dishes of her childhood, he said, only adapt them gently, perhaps with more vegetables, less salt or a lighter hand with the oil. That evening she cooked her grandmother's dumplings and found that they still tasted exactly like home.

Fads, Davit told her, come and go like fashions in hats, and each one arrives with a miraculous promise. A food that claims to cure every illness, or a cleanse that promises to flush out mysterious toxins, usually has someone behind it who is trying to sell something. The body already has a liver and kidneys to do that work, he said, and no single food, however exotic or expensive, can replace a good overall pattern.

Rule twelve, Davit said, was the most important of all, which was to make peace with food. Eating should be a pleasure and not a source of fear, and a person who is constantly anxious about food or whose thoughts about weight dominate their days should speak to a doctor. Help is available for those who need it, he said, and asking for it is always a sign of strength and never of weakness.

Davit added a final caution, which was that his rules were general and could not fit everyone. People with allergies, diabetes, kidney disease or other health conditions, along with pregnant women, growing children and frail older people, may need individual advice from a doctor or a dietitian. For them, the rules are a starting point for a conversation and not a replacement for one.

At the end of the month, Elif found that she was cooking most of her own meals, packing her lunches and eating dinner at a proper table. She felt lighter and more energetic than she had in a long time, though she had not banned a single food, counted a single calorie or bought a single miracle powder. Davit, watching her chop onions with newfound confidence, said that she no longer needed him.

Before she left, Davit wrote the rules on a single page, and it fitted easily. It said to cook, read the back of the packet, go easy on ultra-processed food, fill your plate with plants, drink mostly water, slow down and make peace with food. Elif pinned it to her fridge beside the note with her five meals, and it was not a diet but something better, a way of living that she could actually follow.

As the evening light slanted across Davit's table, Elif and her uncle raised their glasses of water to a month of simple meals and to a lifetime of simple rules. This book has offered only general information, and it is not medical advice, so it cannot take the place of a doctor or a dietitian who understands your own health and your own needs. For everyone else, the invitation is the same one that Davit gave: pick one rule, start with the next meal, and let the rest follow in its own good time.
